title: IP Lecture Drill
heading: Lecture Drill
lede: Practice questions written from your lecture PDFs and the course book, one tab per lecture. Lecture 4 has no slides, so its questions come from the book's Chapter 4 (pp. 80–99). Pick an answer to see at once whether it is right. Each answer has a short explanation and the slide or book page it comes from.
foot: These are practice questions written from your lecture slides and the Image Processing course book (marked "Book"). They are not past exam papers. Progress is saved in this browser only.
source: IP Lec 1-3 slides and Digital Image Processing 27.pdf (Ch 1-4)

questions.text: According to the slides, a picture that is not immediately recognizable is still ......
options: pure noise that should be removed first
not just a random blur: it has structure
useless until it has been segmented
a vector image rather than a raster image
questions.why: An image is a single picture that represents something. Even if it is not immediately recognizable it will not be just a random blur, and that structure is what we improve or analyse.

questions.text: How do the slides relate image processing to computer vision?
options: Computer vision is a subset of image processing
Image processing is a subset of computer vision
The two fields share no algorithms at all
Image processing is a subset of machine learning
questions.why: Slide 4 draws image processing inside computer vision: a computer vision system uses image processing algorithms as building blocks to emulate vision at human scale.

questions.text: Which pair correctly gives the usual output of each field?
options: IP: knowledge of the scene; CV: an image in a different form
IP: a colour map of the scene; CV: an enhanced image
IP: an image in a different form; CV: knowledge of the scene
IP: a list of object labels; CV: a compressed JPEG image file
questions.why: Image processing takes an image and returns an image, usually a better one. Computer vision takes an image and returns knowledge of the scene, such as 'smiling kid'.
questions.ref: Slide 23 · Image processing and computer vision

questions.text: In 'How does a computer see?', the sensors feed an inference system. Which three blocks make up that inference system?
options: Pre-processing, feature extraction, ML model
Sampling, quantization and compression
Image enhancement, restoration and segmentation
Image acquisition, storage and display
questions.why: The computer replaces the eye with sensors and the brain with an inference system: pre-processing, feature extraction and a machine learning model, which outputs labels such as mountain, sun and cloud.
questions.ref: Slide 52 · How does a computer see

questions.text: Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) is given in the slides as a way to ......
options: detect tumours and measure organ sizes
reject unlabelled bottles on a conveyor
control automatic gates and track vehicles
detect road lanes and signs for self-driving cars
questions.why: Slide 9 lists ANPR among the CCTV and traffic uses of computer vision: controlling automatic gates, vehicle tracking, analysing crowds and counting people.

questions.text: Image processing changes the nature of an image to either improve its pictorial information for human interpretation or ......
options: compress it so that it needs far fewer bits to be stored on disk
render it more suitable for autonomous machine perception
convert it from a raster image into a vector image
raise its resolution until the eye sees no pixels
questions.why: These are the two goals in the definition on slide 17 (also in the course book, p. 7): a better picture for people, or an image better suited to a machine.

questions.text: Which of these operations is done mainly to suit a machine rather than a human viewer?
options: Sharpening the edges so the image looks crisper
Removing noise from a speckled photograph
Removing motion blur from a photo of a car
Blurring the image to remove its fine detail
questions.why: Removing detail by blurring, like obtaining the edges, gives an image a person would not prefer, but its large-scale content is easier for a program to analyse. The other three improve the picture for a person.

questions.text: When a scene is digitized, rounding each measured brightness to one of a finite number of levels (for example 0 to 255) is called ......
options: quantization
sampling
interpolation
aliasing
questions.why: Sampling chooses where brightness is measured (the pixel grid); quantization rounds each measured value to one of a finite set of levels. Together they turn the continuous scene into a matrix of numbers.

questions.text: An image of fine stripes is undersampled. What appears in the sampled image?
options: Banding: smooth gradients break into visible flat steps
Noise: random errors added to the pixel values
Aliasing: false, coarser patterns not in the scene
Motion blur: edges smeared in a single direction
questions.why: Too few samples cannot represent the fine stripes, so they show up as false, coarser patterns (aliasing), as in the undersampled swirl on slide 25. Banding comes from too few grey levels, not too few samples.

questions.text: By the Nyquist criterion as the slides state it, what is the largest sample spacing that can capture y = sin(2x) + 0.5 sin(5x)?
options: About 1.26, that is 2π/5
About 1.57, that is π/2
About 3.14, that is π
About 0.63, that is π/5
questions.why: The fastest part is sin(5x), with one cycle every 2π/5 ≈ 1.26. At least two samples per cycle means a spacing of at most π/5 ≈ 0.63. Working from sin(2x) ignores the highest frequency. This follows the slide's 'at least twice'; the lecture page's Check the source note warns that exactly twice can fail (samples every π/5 from x = 0 all land on zeros of sin(5x)), so the strict rule needs a spacing below π/5.

questions.text: The slides' function y = sin(x) + (1/3) sin(3x) is sampled every π/3 starting at x = 0, exactly two samples per cycle of sin(3x). What do the samples show?
options: Only sin(x): each sample falls on a zero of sin(3x)
The whole curve, ripples included, as Nyquist allows
Only sin(3x): each sample falls on a zero of sin(x)
Nothing: every sampled value of y is exactly zero
questions.why: sin(3 · kπ/3) = sin(kπ) = 0, so the samples equal those of sin(x) and the ripple is lost. The slide says 'at least twice'; following the lecture page's Check the source note (Gonzalez and Woods), the rate must exceed twice the highest frequency.

questions.text: Which description fits a CCD camera rather than a CMOS camera?
options: Cheaper and needs less power to run than a CCD
High resolution and robust against noise
More susceptible to noise in the image
Captures the scene one row at a time
questions.why: Slide 28: a CCD produces images with high resolution and is robust against noise. Slide 29: CMOS is cheaper and needs less power but is more susceptible to noise. Row-by-row capture is the flatbed scanner.

questions.text: How does a flatbed scanner capture an image?
options: A large 2-D photosite array captures it all at once
It stores formulas for the shapes it finds in the page
One single sensor cell measures the page column by column
A single row of photosites moves across it, row by row
questions.why: The scanner works on the same principle as the CCD camera, but instead of capturing the whole image at once on a large array, a single row of photosites moves across the image and fills the output row by row.

questions.text: An image f(x, y) is called a digital image when ......
options: x and y are discrete but f can take any real value
it is stored as mathematical formulas for its shapes
it was captured with visible light by a digital camera
x, y and f values are all finite, discrete quantities
questions.why: Slide 38: when x, y and the intensity values of f are all finite, discrete quantities, the image is digital. Its elements are called pixels (also pels, picture elements or image elements).

questions.text: A grayscale image is the matrix f, with rows and columns numbered from 1 as in the lecture's f(r, c). The pixel f(4, 3) is which element in Python with NumPy?
questions.why: The matrix f(r, c) numbers rows and columns from 1 (x and y run from 1 to 256 for a 256 × 256 image), while NumPy indices start at 0, so f(4, 3) is `f[3, 2]`.

questions.text: A vector drawing of a red line from a to b is enlarged to four times its size. What happens to the file size?
options: It grows four times, just like the length of the line
It grows sixteen times, like the drawing's area
It stays the same; the same instructions draw it
It grows, because more pixels must now be stored
questions.why: A vector image stores instructions (dot at a, dot at b, join them, colour the line red), not pixels. Enlarging it only changes the coordinates, so the file size does not change and the line stays smooth.

questions.text: For raster graphics, a photograph must be sampled. What do the slides call this sampling, and what are the samples called?
options: Quantization; the samples are grey levels
Rendering; the samples are vectors
Scanning; the samples are pixels
Indexing; the samples are colour maps
questions.why: A photograph is analog data whose intensity varies in space instead of time, so it must be sampled. For images this sampling is normally called scanning, and the samples are pixels (picture elements).

questions.text: What makes a task image restoration rather than image enhancement?
options: It makes the result more suitable for a particular use
It subdivides the image into its constituent parts
It reduces the number of bits needed to store the image
It reverses damage done to the image by a known cause
questions.why: Slide 49 defines restoration as reversing the damage done by a known cause, such as blur from linear motion, optical distortions or periodic interference. Enhancement (slide 48) only makes the result more suitable for an application.

questions.text: In an aerial photograph, labelling every pixel as car, tree, building or road is an example of ......
options: image restoration
contrast enhancement
image segmentation
image acquisition
questions.why: Segmentation subdivides an image into its constituent parts. Identifying cars, trees, buildings or roads in an aerial photograph, with a class for every pixel, is semantic segmentation.

questions.text: In the slides, which order of steps does an image processing task follow?
options: Acquire, preprocess, segment, represent and describe
Preprocess, acquire, segment, represent and describe
Acquire, segment, preprocess, represent and describe
Acquire, segment, represent and describe, then preprocess
questions.why: Slide 51 lists acquiring the image, preprocessing, segmentation, then representation and description. The course book's diagram (p. 23) puts feature extraction, recognition and interpretation after segmentation instead.

questions.text: In the coin-counting example, why is the thresholded image eroded before the coins are counted?
options: To turn the grayscale image into a binary image
To brighten the dark coins against the background
To make each coin larger so that no small coin is missed
To separate touching coins so each one is counted once
questions.why: Thresholding makes the coins white on black, but touching coins merge into one blob. Erosion shrinks every white region until they come apart, and then the regions are counted (N = 22).

questions.text: Which images does the course book name as suitable for binary representation?
options: Text, fingerprints and architectural plans
Colour photographs of outdoor scenes
Smoothly shaded medical X-ray and CT images
Cartoons and icons with 256 colours
questions.why: A binary pixel is only black or white, so one bit per pixel is enough. That suits text (printed or handwritten), fingerprints and architectural plans; shaded or coloured images need more bits.

questions.text: How many grey levels can a 5-bit grayscale image show?
questions.why: The number of levels is L = 2^k, so 2^5 = 32 levels, from 0 to 31. 31 is the brightest value, not the number of levels.

questions.text: A 512 × 512 binary image is stored with 1 bit per pixel. How many kilobytes does it need (1 KB = 1024 bytes)?
options: 256 KB
4 KB
768 KB
32 KB
questions.why: 512 × 512 × 1 = 262,144 bits; ÷ 8 = 32,768 bytes; ÷ 1024 = 32 KB. Using 8 bits per pixel (or forgetting ÷ 8) gives 256 KB.

questions.text: An indexed image has the colour map `[0 0 0; 1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 1]`, with its rows numbered from 0 as in the course book's figure. A pixel holds the value 2. Which colour is displayed?
options: Red
Green
Blue
Near-black grey
questions.why: The pixel value is an index into the map, not a colour. Counting rows from 0, row 2 is `[0 1 0]`, which is green. Counting from 1 instead would give red.

questions.text: According to the slides, what happens when the scanning resolution is sufficiently high?
options: The eye cannot see the discontinuity between pixels
Each pixel then needs fewer bits of colour depth
Fine patterns in the scene start to turn into aliasing
The file size stops depending on the pixel count
questions.why: Resolution is the scanning rate, how many pixels are recorded per square or linear inch. If it is high enough, the human eye cannot recognize the discontinuity in the reproduced image.

questions.text: What does the colour depth of an image mean?
options: The number of pixels recorded per square or linear inch
The number of bits used to represent a pixel
The number of rows in its colour map
The number of colour channels it has
questions.why: Slide 62: the number of bits used to represent a pixel is its colour depth, and it depends on how the pixel's colour is encoded (1 bit for binary, 8 for grayscale, 24 for True-Color).

questions.text: How much storage does a 256 × 256 grayscale image with 8 bits per pixel need (1 KB = 1024 bytes)?
options: 64 KB
512 KB
192 KB
questions.why: 256 × 256 × 8 / 8 = 65,536 bytes, and 65,536 / 1024 = 64 KB. Forgetting to divide by 8 gives 512 KB.

questions.text: A 1024 × 768 True-Color image is stored without compression. What is its size (1 KB = 1024 bytes)?
options: 768 KB
questions.why: True-Color uses 24 bits (3 bytes) per pixel: 1024 × 768 × 3 = 2,359,296 bytes, and 2,359,296 / 1024 = 2304 KB. With 8 bits per pixel you get 768 KB; forgetting ÷ 8 gives 18,432 KB.

questions.text: An 800 × 600 image is stored as an indexed image with 8-bit indices and a 256-entry colour map at 3 bytes per entry. How many bytes does it need in total?
questions.why: The indices take 800 × 600 × 8 / 8 = 480,000 bytes and the map 256 × 3 = 768 bytes, so 480,768 bytes: about a third of the 1,440,000 bytes the same image needs in True-Color.

questions.text: How do the JPEG and GIF standards encode colour?
options: JPEG: True-Color, compressed; GIF: indexed colour
JPEG: indexed colour; GIF: True-Color, compressed
JPEG and GIF both store plain, uncompressed 24-bit True-Color
JPEG: vector shapes; GIF: one bit for each pixel
questions.why: Slide 66: JPEG uses the True-Color scheme but compresses the image to reduce the number of bits; GIF uses the indexed colour scheme, so a GIF holds at most 256 colours.

questions.text: Averaging each pixel with the pixels around it, or finding edges, uses more than the pixel's own value. What kind of operation is this?
options: A point operation
A neighbourhood operation
A transform operation
A colour-map lookup
questions.why: It uses the pixel's neighbourhood (for example the 3 × 5 block centred on it), so it is a neighbourhood operation; the course book's image filtering (mean, Gaussian, median, Laplacian, Sobel) modifies pixels according to their neighbours. A point operation uses only the pixel's own value.

questions.text: Using Solution 1 (the average of the channels), what is the grey value of a pixel with R = 120, G = 200, B = 85?
questions.why: Solution 1 averages the channels: (120 + 200 + 85) / 3 = 405 / 3 = 135. 163 is what the weighted sum 0.2989R + 0.5870G + 0.1140B gives, and 120 is Solution 2 with the red channel.

questions.text: The grayscale patch `[74 75 120; 30 200 76]` is converted to binary with threshold T = 75. What is the result?
questions.why: A pixel becomes 1 when Gray(i,j) ≥ T and 0 when it is below T. The value 75 is not below 75, so it becomes 1; only 74 and 30 become 0.

questions.text: Thresholding a grayscale image at T turns every pixel into 0 or 1. Which image type results, and how many bits does a pixel then need?
options: Binary, 1 bit per pixel
Grayscale, 8 bits per pixel
Indexed, 8 bits plus a map
RGB, 24 bits per pixel
questions.why: Each pixel becomes 1 where Gray ≥ T and 0 elsewhere, so the result is a binary image, which needs only 1 bit per pixel. The course book lists thresholding among the segmentation techniques.

questions.text: A 240 × 320 grayscale image (8 bits per pixel) is converted to RGB by copying its grey value into all three channels. How many bytes does the 24-bit RGB version take?
questions.why: True-Color stores three 8-bit values (24 bits) per pixel: 240 × 320 × 3 = 230,400 bytes, three times the 76,800 bytes of the grey original, although it shows the same grey picture. 1,843,200 is that size in bits, with the ÷8 forgotten.

questions.text: Image processing operations are divided into point, neighbourhood and transform classes according to ......
options: the number of different grey levels that the image contains
the size of the image in rows and columns
the information needed to compute the new pixel value
the colour model used to store the image file
questions.why: The slides divide operations by the information required to perform the transformation: the pixel alone, a small neighbourhood around it, or the whole image.

questions.text: Which pairing of operation class and the information it needs is correct?
options: Neighbourhood: the grey levels in a small mask around the pixel
Point: the grey levels in a small mask around the pixel
Transform: only the pixel's own grey value, nothing else
Neighbourhood: the whole image, processed together as one single block
questions.why: A point process uses only the pixel's own value, a neighbourhood process uses a small mask around the pixel, and a transform processes the entire image as one large block.

questions.text: In transform processing the image is transformed and then processed in the new form. What step gives back the processed original image?
options: Applying the same transform a second time
Clipping the result to the range 0 to 255
Equalizing the histogram of the result
Applying the inverse transform
questions.why: A transform represents the pixel values in another but equivalent form. After processing in that form, the inverse transform brings the result back to an ordinary image.

questions.text: Which of these is NOT a point operation?
options: Gamma correction
Edge detection
Histogram matching
Colour correction
questions.why: The slides list brightness and contrast adjustment, gamma correction, histogram equalization, histogram matching and colour correction as point operations. Edge detection has to compare a pixel with its neighbours, so it needs neighbourhood processing.

questions.text: Why can a point operation on an 8-bit image be carried out so quickly?
options: It only needs to process the pixels that lie along the image border
Its result for all 256 grey values can be stored in a lookup table
It first converts the whole image into the Fourier domain
It skips every pixel whose value is already 0 or 255
questions.why: The output depends only on the input value, so f can be computed once for the 256 possible values and stored in a lookup table; each pixel then costs one table lookup.
questions.ref: Book p. 37 · Point operations and lookup tables

questions.text: Histogram equalization builds its mapping from the histogram of the whole image. Why is it still a point operation?
options: Every pixel of the image is changed by the same constant amount
Each pixel is replaced by the average of its 3 × 3 neighbourhood
The image is processed in the frequency domain and then transformed back
Each new value depends only on the pixel's own old value
questions.why: A point operation is y = f(x): the new value is a function of the pixel's value alone. Equalization only uses the histogram to choose f; after that every pixel of grey level i becomes j, whatever its neighbours are.

questions.text: An 8-bit pixel of value 90 has 128 subtracted from it, with rounding and clipping. What is the result?
questions.why: 90 − 128 = −38, which is below 0, so it is clipped to 0. (218 is what uint8 wrap-around modulo 256 would give, as in NumPy.)

questions.text: The pixels `[100 130 180 250]` of an 8-bit image have 128 added to them, with clipping. What do they become?
questions.why: 100 + 128 = 228, while 258, 308 and 378 are above 255 and are all clipped to 255. Clipping destroys information: those three different pixels can no longer be told apart.
questions.ref: Slide 10 · Adding and subtracting a constant

questions.text: How does multiplying an image by a constant C > 1 differ from adding a constant to it?
options: It brightens every pixel by exactly the same amount as adding C
It darkens the image and squeezes the grey levels closer together
It turns the image into its negative, swapping dark and light
It brightens and spreads the grey levels apart, raising contrast
questions.why: y = Cx with C > 1 brightens, and because the gaps between grey levels are multiplied by C the contrast rises too. Adding a constant only shifts every grey level by the same amount: in g = a·f + b, the slope a controls contrast and the intercept b controls brightness.

questions.text: In MATLAB, `immultiply(b, 0.5)` is applied to a `uint8` pixel of value 73. What is the result?
questions.why: 73 × 0.5 = 36.5, and the `uint8` result must be rounded to an integer. MATLAB, like the hand method, rounds a half upward, giving 37. NumPy's `np.round` would give 36, because it rounds a half to the nearest even integer.

questions.text: The function y = x/2 + 128 maps the full grey range 0–255 onto which range, and what is its drawback?
options: 128–255, brightening but clipping every one of the bright pixels
0–127, darkening the image while keeping its contrast
128–255, brightening without clipping but lowering contrast
64–191, raising the contrast of the mid-tones of the image
questions.why: Halving squeezes 0–255 into 0–127.5, and adding 128 lifts that to 128–255.5, so the result fills 128–255 with no real clipping (only 255 itself rounds to 256 and is cut back by one level). But the grey levels are packed half as far apart, so contrast drops.

questions.text: Which MATLAB call computes y = x/2 + 128 on the `uint8` image `b`?
options: `immultiply(imadd(b,128),0.5)`
`imadd(immultiply(b,0.5),128)`
`imadd(imdivide(b,0.5),128)`
`imsubtract(immultiply(b,2),128)`
questions.why: Halve first with `immultiply(b,0.5)` (or `imdivide(b,2)`), then add 128 with `imadd`. Adding first would clip at 255 before halving, and `imdivide(b,0.5)` doubles the image.

questions.text: The slides show `b1 = b + 128` on a `uint8` image failing with an error. What does it do in current MATLAB versions?
options: It works and clips at 255, just like `imadd`
It wraps around modulo 256, so 200 becomes 72
It still fails: + is not defined for class uint8
It silently converts the result to class double
questions.why: The error on the slide comes from old MATLAB versions, as the lecture page notes. Current versions saturate integer arithmetic, so `b + 128` clips at 255 like `imadd`; wrapping modulo 256 is what NumPy does.
questions.ref: Slide 11 · Adding and subtracting a constant

questions.text: What is the complement of the grey value 37 in an 8-bit image?
questions.why: y = 255 − x = 255 − 37 = 218. (219 comes from wrongly using 256 instead of 255 = L − 1, and −218 from subtracting the wrong way round.)

questions.text: Solarization here complements only the pixels of grey value 128 or less. What does it give for the pixels `[40 128 129 200]`?
questions.why: 40 becomes 255 − 40 = 215 and 128 becomes 127; 129 and 200 are above 128 and stay as they are. Complementing every pixel would also turn 129 into 126 and 200 into 55.

questions.text: For a `double` image with values in [0, 1], what does `imcomplement` compute?
questions.why: `imcomplement` works for every image type: 255 − x for uint8, 1 − x for double images in [0, 1], and it swaps 0 and 1 in a binary image.

questions.text: How is the histogram of an image with L grey levels represented?
options: A two-dimensional array the same size as the image, holding each grey level
A one-dimensional array of L elements; element k counts the pixels of level k
A one-dimensional array of L elements; element k counts the pixels up to level k
A one-dimensional array listing the positions of the L brightest pixels
questions.why: The histogram gives the frequency of each brightness value: element k holds n_k, the number of pixels with grey level k. Counting the pixels up to level k gives the cumulative histogram instead.

questions.text: The slides' histogram algorithm starts by setting every element of the array `hf` to zero. What is the next step?
options: For every pixel (x, y) of f, increment `hf[f(x,y)]` by 1
For every pixel (x, y) of f, set `hf[x,y]` equal to f(x, y)
For every grey level k, add the value k to `hf[k]`
For every pixel (x, y) of f, add f(x, y) to `hf[0]`
questions.why: Each pixel adds one to the bin of its own grey level, so after one pass over the image `hf[k]` holds the number of pixels with grey level k.

questions.text: What is the histogram, for levels 0 to 7, of the 8-level image `[3 3 4 2; 3 4 4 5; 2 3 4 3; 4 2 3 5]`?
questions.why: Counting the 16 pixels gives three 2s, six 3s, five 4s and two 5s. The list 0 0 3 9 14 16 16 16 is the cumulative histogram, not the histogram.

questions.text: Which pairing of histogram shape and image appearance is correct?
options: Bars crowded at the high end of the scale: a dark image
Bars crowded at the low end of the scale: a dark image
A narrow cluster in the middle of the scale: a high-contrast image
Bars spread evenly over the whole scale: a low-contrast image
questions.why: A dark image has its bins at the low (dark) end and a light image at the high end. A narrow cluster in the middle means low contrast, and bars spread over the whole range mean high contrast.

questions.text: The slides stretch grey levels 5–9 to 2–14 with j = (14 − 2)/(9 − 5) × (i − 5) + 2. What does grey level 8 become?
questions.why: The slope is 12/4 = 3, so j = 3 × (8 − 5) + 2 = 11. The full table is 5→2, 6→5, 7→8, 8→11 and 9→14.

questions.text: After the slides' stretch of levels 5–9 onto 2–14, what happens to the heights of the five crowded histogram bars?
options: They become equal, giving a flat (uniform) histogram
Each bar splits into three bars one level apart
They keep their heights; the bars only move apart
Each bar's height is divided by the slope of 3
questions.why: Stretching maps each grey level to one new grey level, so it moves bars without splitting or merging them: they keep their heights and are now three levels apart instead of one.

questions.text: An image's grey values occupy [60, 180]. Stretched linearly to [0, 255], what does a pixel of value 100 become?
For a `double` image, `imadjust(x,[0.2 0.6],[0.1 0.9])` maps x = 0.1 and x = 0.5 to ......
The grey values of the `uint8` image `pout.tif` lie roughly between 75 and 160. Which call stretches that range to the full range?
questions.why: `imadjust` takes its ranges on a [0, 1] scale, so 75–160 is written `[75 160]/255` and mapped to `[0 1]`. Swapping the two ranges would squeeze the image into 75–160 instead.

questions.text: With gamma correction over the full range, y = 255 × (x/255)^γ. What does a pixel of value 100 become when γ = 0.5?
questions.why: 255 × (100/255)^0.5 = 255 × 0.626 ≈ 159.7, which rounds to 160. The value rises, as expected for γ < 1; γ = 2 would give 39 instead.

questions.text: In `imadjust(im,[a b],[c d],gamma)`, what does a gamma greater than 1 do?
options: Bends the curve upward, so the image becomes brighter
Keeps the straight line between (a, c) and (b, d)
Bends the curve downward, so the image becomes darker
Reverses the curve, so the image turns into its own negative
questions.why: With γ > 1 the power curve sags below the straight line, so mid-tones drop and the image darkens while detail in the bright areas is spread out. γ < 1 brightens and γ = 1 is the linear stretch.

questions.text: In `imadjust(t,[],[],0.5)`, what do the two empty brackets `[]` mean?
options: The input range is found automatically by `stretchlim`
Both the input and the output range are [0, 1]
The output is limited to the range [0, 0.5]
The image is left unchanged and gamma is ignored
questions.why: An empty `[a,b]` or `[c,d]` means [0, 1], so `imadjust(t,[],[],0.5)` applies a gamma of 0.5 over the full range, which brightens the dark tire.

questions.text: A piecewise linear function passes through (0, 0), (64, 20), (192, 235) and (255, 255). What does a pixel of value 96 become?
The slides' stretching function passes through (0, 0), (5, 2), (9, 14) and (15, 15). Which statement about its pieces is correct?
options: The first piece has slope 3 and spreads levels 0–5 apart
The middle piece has slope 1/3 and squeezes levels 5–9 together
The middle piece has slope 3 and spreads levels 5–9 apart
The last piece has slope 1 and leaves levels 9–15 unchanged
questions.why: The slopes are 2/5 = 0.4, 12/4 = 3 and 1/6. A slope above 1 stretches grey levels apart (the middle, where the pixels are) and a slope below 1 compresses them (the nearly empty ends).

questions.text: What does histogram equalization try to produce, and how much user input does it need?
options: A uniform histogram, but the user must choose a and b
A narrower histogram, with the user choosing gamma
The same histogram shape, moved to the bright end
A uniform histogram, with no user input at all
questions.why: Every stretching method needs user input (a, b, γ or breakpoints). Equalization is entirely automatic and aims for a histogram in which every grey level occurs with the same frequency.

questions.text: In the slides' equalization example (L = 16, n = 360), the cumulative count at grey level 9 is 85. What are its scaled value and new grey level?
options: 3.65, so the new level is 4
3.54, so the new level is 3
0.24, so the new level is 0
3.54, so the new level is 4
questions.why: (L − 1)/n × 85 = (15/360) × 85 = 85/24 = 3.54, which rounds to 4. The slide prints 3.65, a misprint the lecture page corrects; the new level 4 is not affected.

questions.text: A 3-bit image (L = 8) of 64 pixels has n_k = 0, 0, 10, 24, 18, 8, 4, 0 for levels 0 to 7. After equalization, what do levels 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 become?
questions.why: The cumulative sums 10, 34, 52, 60, 64 times (L − 1)/n = 7/64 give 1.09, 3.72, 5.69, 6.56 and 7, which round to 1, 4, 6, 7 and 7. Levels 5 and 6 merge at 7.

questions.text: Why is the histogram after equalization usually only approximately flat?
options: All pixels of a grey level move together, so a bar can never split
MATLAB clips the equalized values at 255, piling pixels into the top bar
The cumulative distribution never quite reaches 1 at the last grey level
The darkest grey levels are mapped without any rounding at all
questions.why: Equalization maps grey level to grey level, so bars can be spread apart or merged but never split. A tall bar stays tall, so the histogram can only approach a uniform one.

questions.text: Which statement correctly compares histogram equalization with contrast stretching?
options: Equalization is linear and always keeps the shape of the original histogram
Stretching is non-linear and follows the cumulative histogram
Equalization is non-linear and has a higher risk of over-enhancing noise
Stretching carries the higher risk of an unnatural, noisy result
questions.why: Stretching is a linear min–max mapping that keeps the histogram's shape, with low risk. Equalization follows the cumulative histogram non-linearly and can over-enhance noise and look unnatural.

questions.text: By default, MATLAB's `histeq(p)` aims for a flat histogram with how many grey levels?
questions.why: By default `histeq` targets 64 grey levels: it chooses the mapping whose cumulative histogram comes closest to that of a flat 64-level histogram, so the output has at most 64 distinct values. That is why the bars in the slide's equalized histogram are spaced out.
questions.ref: Slide 25 · Final result of histogram equalization

questions.text: The values stored in a spatial filter mask are called ......
options: pixels
coefficients
grey levels
intensity values
questions.why: Slide 2: the entries of a filter sub-image are coefficients, not pixels. Each coefficient multiplies the image pixel that lies under it.

questions.text: Using correlation (the mask laid directly on the pixels), filter the centre of the neighbourhood `[1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9]` with the slide-4 mask `[1 3 1; 2 4 -2; -3 1 4]`. What is the output?
questions.why: Multiply each pixel by the coefficient on top of it and add: 1×1 + 3×2 + 1×3 + 2×4 + 4×5 − 2×6 − 3×7 + 1×8 + 4×9 = 49. Rotating the mask by 180° first (convolution) would give 61.

questions.text: Compute the true convolution output at the centre of `[4 1 0; 2 3 5; 6 0 7]` with the mask `[1 2 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 3]`.
questions.why: Convolution rotates the mask by 180° to `[3 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 2 1]`, then multiplies and adds: 3×4 + 1×3 + 2×0 + 1×7 = 22. Laying the unrotated mask on the pixels (correlation) gives 30.

questions.text: True convolution uses f(x − s, y − t) where correlation uses f(x + s, y + t). In practice, this means the mask is ...... before it is laid on the image.
options: rotated by 180°
negated (signs flipped)
transposed
rotated by 90°
questions.why: Replacing s and t by −s and −t reverses the mask both top to bottom and left to right, which is a 180° rotation. The products are then summed exactly as in correlation.

questions.text: For which masks do correlation and convolution give exactly the same output?
options: Any mask whose coefficients add up to exactly 1
Symmetric masks, like the mean or Laplacian
Only masks with no negative coefficients
Any odd-sized mask, such as a 3×3 or 5×5 one
questions.why: A symmetric mask looks the same after a 180° rotation, so the two operations coincide. A single off-centre 1 also sums to 1, yet it shifts the image in opposite directions under correlation and convolution.

questions.text: With no extra options, what does MATLAB's `imfilter(f, h)` do?
options: Correlates, zero-pads and keeps the size
Convolves, zero-pads and keeps the size
Correlates and keeps only where the mask fits
Convolves and replicates the border pixels
questions.why: By default `imfilter` uses correlation with zero padding and returns an image the same size as `f`; add the `'conv'` option to convolve. `conv2` is the function that convolves.

questions.text: What does filtering an image with `[0 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 0]` give?
options: The same image, unchanged
The image shifted by one pixel
A slightly blurred copy
A black image with one bright pixel
questions.why: A single 1 at the centre is the discrete impulse (delta). By the sifting property it copies each pixel's own value, so it is the identity filter.
questions.ref: Slide 14 · Delta function as the mask

questions.text: Slide 9 convolves an image with `[0 0 0; 1 0 0; 0 0 0]`. What is the result?
options: The image shifted right by one pixel
The image blurred along each row
The image unchanged, as one 1 is kept
The image shifted left by one pixel
questions.why: Convolution rotates the mask, which moves the 1 to the right of centre, so each output pixel copies its right-hand neighbour. The picture therefore moves one pixel to the left.

questions.text: A 200×300 image is filtered with a 7×7 mask that must stay inside the image (no padding). What is the output size?
questions.why: Without padding the output is (M − m + 1) × (N − n + 1) = (200 − 7 + 1) × (300 − 7 + 1) = 194×294. Padding by (7 − 1)/2 = 3 pixels on every side would keep 200×300.

questions.text: A 6×6 image in which every pixel is 90 is filtered with the 3×3 mean filter using zero padding. What is the output at a corner pixel?
questions.why: At a corner only 4 of the 9 window pixels lie inside the image, so the output is 4 × 90 / 9 = 40 (an edge pixel gives 6 × 90 / 9 = 60). These dark borders are the artefacts of zero padding; replicate padding would keep 90.

questions.text: Which border method fills the missing neighbours with pixels from the opposite side of the image, and suits periodic data?
options: Replicate
Zero padding
Symmetric (mirror)
Wrap around
questions.why: Wrap around treats the image as if it repeats, taking values from the opposite edge; the book recommends it for periodic or seamless data. Replicate copies the nearest border pixel and mirror reflects the image.

questions.text: A filtered image `g` has values from −50 to 200, and `imshow(g, [])` scales that range to [0, 255] for display. At what grey level is a pixel of value 50 shown?
questions.why: Scaling uses y = 255 × (x − gL) / (gH − gL) = 255 × (50 + 50) / (200 + 50) = 102. Clipping would have left 50 as it is.

questions.text: What mask does `h = fspecial('average', 11)` create?
options: An 11×11 mask with every coefficient 1/11
An 11×11 mask of ones that adds up to 121
An 11×11 mask with every coefficient 1/121
A 1×11 row mask with every coefficient 1/11
questions.why: An n×n averaging mask has n² equal coefficients of 1/n², here 1/121, so they add up to 1. The slides then apply it with `imfilter(in_image, h)`.

questions.text: The slides blur the same photo with averaging masks of size 11, 15 and 21. What happens as the mask gets bigger?
options: Nothing changes, since the coefficients sum to 1
The image gets brighter, as more pixels are added
The blur gets weaker, as each coefficient is smaller
The blur gets stronger and more detail is lost
questions.why: Slide 11: a larger window averages over more pixels, so the smoothing increases. The coefficients still add up to 1, so flat areas keep their brightness.
questions.ref: Slide 11 · Effect of average filter size

questions.text: A single salt pixel (255) sits on a flat background of 30. After a 3×3 mean filter, what value do the 9 pixels of its neighbourhood take?
questions.why: Each of those windows holds the one 255 and eight 30s: (8 × 30 + 255) / 9 = 55. The impulse is spread into a grey 3×3 blotch, which is why averaging handles salt-and-pepper noise badly; a median would return 30.

questions.text: A separable 9×9 mask is applied as a column pass and then a row pass. How many additions does each output pixel need?
questions.why: After separation an N×N mask needs 2N multiplications and 2N − 2 additions: 2 × 9 − 2 = 16. Applied directly it needs 81 multiplications and 80 additions.

questions.text: A separable mask is the column `[1; 2; 1]` times the row `[1 0 -1]`. Which 3×3 mask is it?
questions.why: The outer product multiplies the row by each entry of the column in turn: 1 × [1 0 −1], 2 × [1 0 −1], 1 × [1 0 −1]. Swapping the two vectors would give the transposed mask instead.
questions.ref: Slide 18 · Separable masks as outer products

questions.text: A separable mask h equals a column vector c times a row vector r. Which property of convolution lets you filter with c and then with r instead of once with h?
options: Associativity
Distributivity
Isotropy
Commutativity
questions.why: Associativity gives f * (c * r) = (f * c) * r, so two simple 1-D passes equal one pass with the full mask. This is what makes separable filters cheaper.

questions.text: In this lecture, the frequency of an image region measures ......
options: how often each grey level appears in the image
how much the grey values change with distance
how many pixels the image holds per unit length
how bright the region is on average
questions.why: Slide 19: frequency is a measure of the amount by which grey values change with distance. Large changes over small distances (edges, detail, noise) are high frequency; smooth areas are low frequency.

questions.text: Which of these masks is a low-pass (smoothing) filter?
questions.why: Its coefficients are all positive and add up to 16/16 = 1, so flat regions stay unchanged while changes are smoothed. The other three add up to 0, so they are high-pass masks that respond only to change.

questions.text: In the Gaussian filter, what does a larger standard deviation σ do?
options: It sharpens edges instead of smoothing them
It gives the centre pixel even more weight
It turns the Gaussian into a non-linear filter
It blurs more and removes fine detail
questions.why: σ sets the width of the bell curve: a small σ gives slight smoothing, a large σ a strong blur that removes fine details. A wider bell spreads the weight away from the centre.

questions.text: The Laplacian is a ...... operator.
options: rank-order (sorting)
second-order derivative
smoothing (local averaging)
first-order derivative
questions.why: Slide 22: ∇²f = ∂²f/∂x² + ∂²f/∂y², a sum of second derivatives, each approximated by differences of neighbours to give h1. Sobel masks, by contrast, are first-order derivatives.

questions.text: Apply the Laplacian mask h1 = `[0 1 0; 1 -4 1; 0 1 0]` at the centre of `[3 9 3; 7 12 5; 3 11 3]`. What is the response?
questions.why: Only the four direct neighbours count: 9 + 7 + 5 + 11 − 4 × 12 = 32 − 48 = −16. The mask h2 = −h1 would give +16, and the 8-neighbour mask h3 gives −52.

questions.text: Sharpen the centre of `[40 50 40; 30 60 70; 40 20 40]` with the single mask `[0 -1 0; -1 5 -1; 0 -1 0]`. What is the new value?
Why add the diagonal neighbours, as in h3 = `[1 1 1; 1 -8 1; 1 1 1]`, to the Laplacian?
options: It becomes isotropic in 45° steps, not 90°
It can then be split into two 1-D masks
It becomes much less sensitive to image noise
Its coefficients then add up to 1, so it smooths
questions.why: h1 treats x and y alike (isotropic for 90° rotations); including the diagonals gives isotropic results for increments of 45° (slide 23). Its coefficients still add up to 0, so it is still high-pass.

questions.text: The directional mask `[-1 0 1; -1 0 1; -1 0 1]` responds mainly to ...... edges.
options: all directions equally
vertical
horizontal
diagonal
questions.why: It subtracts the left column from the right one, so a vertical edge such as `[0 9 9; 0 9 9; 0 9 9]` gives 27, while a horizontal edge gives 0. The mask `[-1 -1 -1; 0 0 0; 1 1 1]` finds horizontal edges and `[-1 -1 0; -1 0 1; 0 1 1]` diagonal ones.

questions.text: Unsharp masking (edge crispening) is based on ......
options: replacing each pixel by its window's median
adding a blurred copy of the image to the image
multiplying the image by a boost coefficient
subtracting a blurred copy from the image
questions.why: Slide 30: unsharp masking subtracts a blurred version of an image from the image itself. What remains is the detail that the blur removed.

questions.text: Slide 30 labels `f - blur(f)` as the sharpened image. What is `f - blur(f)` on its own?
options: The original image shifted by one pixel
A high-pass image in which flat regions become 0
A low-pass image that is smoother than the original
A sharpened image that is ready to display as is
questions.why: Every flat region gives `f - blur(f)` = 0, so alone it looks like an edge map; the sharpening comes from adding it back to f. The slides call it the sharpened image; this follows the lecture page's Check-the-source note.

questions.text: Each row of an image is 20 20 20 110 110. A 3×3 mean filter is applied. What is `f - blur(f)` at the three interior pixels?
questions.why: The mean blurs the interior pixels to (20+20+20)/3 = 20, (20+20+110)/3 = 50 and (20+110+110)/3 = 80, so f − blur is 20 − 20 = 0, 20 − 50 = −30 and 110 − 80 = 30. Adding this to f gives the dip and overshoot of slide 31.

questions.text: High-boost filtering uses `fhb = A*f - blur(f)`. At a pixel with f = 100 and blur(f) = 70, what is the output for A = 1.5?
questions.why: 1.5 × 100 − 70 = 150 − 70 = 80, the same as (A − 1) f + fs = 0.5 × 100 + 30. With A = 1 only the difference, 30, would remain.

questions.text: In the slides' high-boost demo with h = `[0 -1 0; -1 A+4 -1; 0 -1 0]`, how does A = 1.7 compare with A = 1?
options: Darker, because less of f is kept
Only the edges remain on grey
Still sharp, but much brighter
Blurrier, because A > 1 smooths
questions.why: fhb = (A − 1) f + fs, so A > 1 adds extra original on top of the sharpening and raises the overall brightness (slide 34). A = 0 gives the Laplacian alone and A = 1 ordinary Laplacian sharpening.

questions.text: What does a rank-order filter do at each mask position?
options: Averages the values, giving the centre pixel the largest weight
Sorts the window and returns the value at a chosen rank
Subtracts a blurred copy of the window from its centre value
Multiplies the values by coefficients and adds the products
questions.why: Slide 35: the elements under the mask are ordered and a particular value is returned. Max, min and median are all rank-order filters, which makes them non-linear.

questions.text: A 3×3 window holds `[21 18 200; 19 0 22; 20 23 17]`. What does the median filter put at its centre?
questions.why: Sorted: 0, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 200; the middle (5th) value is 20. The mean, 340/9 ≈ 37.8, is dragged up by the outlier 200.

questions.text: Apply an alpha-trimmed mean that trims two values from each end to the 3×3 window `[16 0 11; 255 12 5; 9 20 17]`. What is the result?
questions.why: Sorted: 0, 5, 9, 11, 12, 16, 17, 20, 255. Drop 0, 5, 20 and 255, then average the rest: (9 + 11 + 12 + 16 + 17) / 5 = 65 / 5 = 13. The median is 12, the plain mean 38.3, and dividing by 9 instead of 5 gives 7.2.

questions.text: Why does the median filter remove salt-and-pepper noise so well?
options: It averages each impulse with its neighbours until it fades
It finds the noisy pixels and sets each of them to zero
Noisy values are extreme, so sorting puts them at the ends
Its negative coefficients cancel the bright and dark impulses
questions.why: Salt (255) and pepper (0) pixels land at the ends of the sorted list, so the middle value comes from real pixels unless more than half the window is noise. Averaging instead mixes the impulses into the result.

questions.text: The slides run `medfilt2(in_image, [21, 21])` on a skin image with hairs. What does the result show?
options: Everything is blurred evenly, outline included
The hairs are gone but the skin outline is kept
The hairs are sharpened and the skin is unchanged
Only the edges remain, on a dark background
questions.why: `medfilt2` replaces each pixel by the median of its 21×21 neighbourhood. Thin hairs are a minority in each window and vanish, while the median keeps edges because its output is always a real value from the window.

questions.text: Frequency in an image roughly describes the rate of change of the pixel values. Which image content therefore belongs to the high frequencies?
options: Edges, fine detail and noise
Smooth areas and gradual lighting
The mean brightness of the image
Large regions of constant grey
questions.why: Edges, fine detail and noise change quickly from pixel to pixel, so they are high frequencies. Smooth areas, lighting and the mean change slowly or not at all, so they are low frequencies.
questions.ref: Book p. 83 · High and low frequencies

questions.text: According to Fourier theory, as the book puts it, any complicated signal can be decomposed into ......
options: a product of complex exponentials that all share one frequency
a sum of step functions with different heights and positions
a single sinusoid whose amplitude slowly changes with time
a sum of sinusoids with different frequencies and amplitudes
questions.why: Fourier's idea is that a complex signal is a sum of simple sines and cosines with different frequencies and amplitudes. The Fourier transform is what breaks the signal into these frequency components.

questions.text: Using the book's 1-D DFT `F[k] = Σ f[n] e^(-j2πkn/N)`, what is F[0] for `f = [2 5 1 4]`?
questions.why: For k = 0 every exponential is `e^0 = 1`, so F[0] = 2 + 5 + 1 + 4 = 12: the sum of the samples, N times their mean of 3. The book's forward formula has no 1/N, so 3 is wrong; -6 is F[2].

questions.text: With N = 4, the book's DFT kernel `e^(-j2πn/4)` for k = 1 takes the values `1, -j, -1, j` for n = 0 to 3. What is F[1] for `f = [1 2 3 4]`?
questions.why: F[1] = 1·1 + 2·(-j) + 3·(-1) + 4·j = 1 - 2j - 3 + 4j = -2 + 2j. Using +j in the exponent, the inverse's sign, would give -2 - 2j instead; -2 is F[2].

questions.text: For a signal of N = 4 samples, which DFT index k stands for the highest frequency the samples can hold?
options: k = 0, the sum term
k = 1, one cycle
questions.why: k = N/2 = 2 is a pattern that flips at every sample: `[3 1 3 1]` has DFT `[8 0 4 0]`, all its non-DC weight at k = 2. k = 3 is only the mirror image of k = 1, the slow cycle.

questions.text: `F = [10, -2+2j, -2, -2-2j]` is the book-style DFT of a 4-sample signal. Using the inverse `f[n] = (1/N) Σ F[k] e^(j2πkn/N)`, what is f[0]?
questions.why: For n = 0 every exponential is 1, so f[0] = (10 - 2 + 2j - 2 - 2 - 2j)/4 = 4/4 = 1. Forgetting the 1/N gives 4; the signal was `[1 2 3 4]`.

questions.text: With the 1/MN in the forward 2-D transform, as in the book's property `F(0,0) = (1/MN) ΣΣ f(x,y)`, what is F(0,0) of the image `[10 20; 30 40]`?
questions.why: F(0,0) = (10 + 20 + 30 + 40)/(2·2) = 100/4 = 25, the mean intensity. 100 is the plain sum, which MATLAB's `fft2` returns because it keeps the 1/MN in `ifft2` instead.

questions.text: One coefficient of a 2-D DFT is `F(u,v) = 3 - 4j`. What is the spectrum value |F(u,v)| there?
questions.why: `|F| = [R² + I²]^(1/2) = √(9 + 16) = 5`. 25 forgets the square root, 7 adds |R| and |I|, and -1 adds R and I.

questions.text: The magnitude |F(u,v)| tells how strong each frequency is in the image. What does the phase angle φ(u,v) determine?
options: The mean brightness of the whole image
The cutoff frequency that a filter should use
How many frequencies the image contains
The positions of the structures in the image
questions.why: The book: the magnitude indicates how strong a frequency is, and the phase `φ = tan^(-1)(I/R)` determines the positioning of structures. The mean brightness is the DC term F(0,0).

questions.text: For a real image, the DFT coefficient at (u, v) = (1, 2) is `3 + 4j`. Using `F(u,v) = F*(-u,-v)`, what is F(-1,-2)?
questions.why: Conjugate symmetry: F(-1,-2) is the complex conjugate of F(1,2), so only the imaginary part changes sign, giving 3 - 4j. Both points have the same magnitude, 5.

questions.text: A 256 × 512 image (M = 256 rows, N = 512 columns) is multiplied by `(-1)^(x+y)` before the transform. Where does the DC term end up?
options: At (0, 0), the top-left corner
At (255, 511), the last corner
questions.why: Multiplying by `(-1)^(x+y)` shifts the centre of the transform to (M/2, N/2) = (128, 256). (256, 128) swaps M and N.

questions.text: The book prints the factor 1/MN in its formula for F(u,v) on p. 83 and again in its 2-D inverse DFT for f(x,y) on p. 84. What does the lecture's correction say?
options: Keep both, so each direction divides by MN
Exactly once; the lecture keeps it in the forward one
Drop both: a 2-D DFT pair needs no scale factor
Keep it only in the inverse, so that F(0,0) is the mean
questions.why: Used in both directions it would divide by MN twice, so it must appear exactly once (the p. 83 formula for F(u,v) is the forward transform, although the book labels it the IDFT). The lecture keeps it in the forward transform, which makes the book's `F(0,0) = (1/MN) ΣΣ f(x,y)` the mean; with it in the inverse, as in `fft2`/`ifft2`, F(0,0) is the sum. This follows the lecture's Check the source note.

questions.text: In a centred spectrum, where do the edges, noise and fine details of the image show up?
options: In a single bright point at the centre
Only along the main diagonal of the array
Mixed evenly over the whole spectrum
Toward the outer edges of the spectrum
questions.why: In a centred spectrum the low frequencies (smooth areas) are at the centre and the high frequencies (edges, noise, fine details) lie toward its edges. The bright centre is the DC term and the other low frequencies.

questions.text: The book's headline advantage: convolution `f(x,y) * h(x,y)` in the spatial domain becomes ...... in the frequency domain.
options: another convolution, of F(u,v) with H(u,v)
element-by-element multiplication, F · H
the sum F(u,v) + H(u,v) at each frequency
the division F(u,v) / H(u,v) at each point
questions.why: The convolution theorem: `f * h ⟺ F · H`. Sliding a mask and summing products in space is the same as multiplying the two transforms frequency by frequency.

questions.text: The lecture counts about `3·log2(MN) + 1` operations per pixel for frequency filtering (three FFTs and one product). How many is that for a 512 × 512 image?
questions.why: MN = 512·512 = 2^18, so log2(MN) = 18 and 3·18 + 1 = 55 operations per pixel, whatever the mask size. 28 wrongly uses log2(512) = 9.
questions.ref: Book p. 80 · Speed for large filters

questions.text: An m × m mask costs m² operations per pixel in space; the frequency route costs `3·log2(MN) + 1`. On a 128 × 128 image, what is the smallest odd mask for which the frequency route is cheaper?
questions.why: log2(128·128) = 14, so the frequency route costs 3·14 + 1 = 43 per pixel. A 5 × 5 mask costs 25, still cheaper in space, while 7 × 7 costs 49 > 43. 9 × 9 is the answer for a 512 × 512 image.
questions.ref: Book p. 80 · Speed for large filters

questions.text: Why is periodic noise much easier to remove in the frequency domain than in the spatial domain?
options: It becomes a few isolated bright spikes that can be zeroed
It is all collected in the DC term, which is easy to subtract
It disappears by itself once fftshift has centred the spectrum
It only affects the phase, so the magnitude stays clean
questions.why: In the image the noise is spread over every pixel, but in the spectrum it is just a few isolated spikes, and setting them to zero removes it. The lecture gives it as an example of the tasks the book calls impossible to perform any other way.
questions.ref: Book p. 80 · Why the frequency domain

questions.text: At one frequency the image transform is `F(u,v) = 40 - 20j` and the filter value is `H(u,v) = 0.25`. What is G(u,v) in the model `G = HF`?
questions.why: `G = H·F = 0.25·(40 - 20j) = 10 - 5j`. The real filter value scales both the real and the imaginary part of that frequency.
questions.ref: Book p. 86 · Filtering model G = HF

questions.text: According to the book, what does attenuating the low frequencies of an image do in the spatial domain?
options: It enhances the edges
It makes the image smoother
It brightens the whole image
It shifts the image to the centre
questions.why: Attenuating high frequencies gives a smoother image; attenuating low frequencies enhances the edges. Removing the low frequencies also removes the mean, so the result gets darker, not brighter.

questions.text: A circular low-pass mask around (M/2, N/2) is multiplied with a spectrum that was never shifted, so its DC term is still at (0, 0). What does the mask keep?
options: The low frequencies, as intended
Only the DC term at the corner
Every frequency, unchanged
The highest frequencies instead
questions.why: Without the shift the low frequencies sit in the four corners and the centre holds the highest ones, so a centred disc keeps exactly the wrong frequencies. That is why the transform is shifted to put the DC coefficient in the centre before filtering.

questions.text: What causes the ringing artefacts that the ideal low-pass filter produces?
options: Its transfer function drops abruptly from 1 to 0 at D0
It keeps the DC term, which adds ripples around every edge
It is applied to a centred rather than an uncentred spectrum
Its cutoff D0 is chosen too large, letting too much noise pass
questions.why: Ringing comes from a transfer function that changes abruptly. The inverse transform of a sharp-edged disc has rings of alternating sign, and convolution echoes them around every edge; the smoother Butterworth and Gaussian filters ring less.

questions.text: An 8 × 8 centred spectrum has its centre at (4, 4) and cutoff D0 = 2. What is the Butterworth low-pass value of order n = 2 at (u, v) = (5, 5)?
questions.why: D = √(1² + 1²) ≈ 1.41, so `(D/D0)^(2n) = (1.41/2)^4 = 0.25` and H = 1/(1 + 0.25) = 0.8. Using the power n instead of 2n gives 0.67, 0.78 is the Gaussian value, and 0.2 is the high-pass 1 - 0.8.

questions.text: Same 8 × 8 spectrum, centre (4, 4), D0 = 2. What does the Gaussian low-pass filter `H = e^(-D²/2D0²)` give at (u, v) = (6, 6)?
questions.why: D² = 2² + 2² = 8, so H = e^(-8/(2·4)) = e^(-1) ≈ 0.37. Dropping the 2 in 2·D0² gives e^(-2) ≈ 0.14, a wrong sign gives e^(+1) ≈ 2.72, and 0.63 is the high-pass value.

questions.text: Same 8 × 8 spectrum, centre (4, 4), D0 = 2. What does the Gaussian high-pass filter `H = 1 - e^(-D²/2D0²)` give at (u, v) = (0, 4)?
questions.why: D = 4, so the low-pass part is e^(-16/8) = e^(-2) ≈ 0.14 and H = 1 - 0.14 ≈ 0.86. Dropping the 2 in 2·D0² gives 1 - e^(-4) ≈ 0.98, and 0.06 is the Butterworth low-pass value there.

questions.text: A Butterworth low-pass filter of order n = 5 is evaluated exactly at its cutoff, D = D0. What is H there?
questions.why: At D = D0 the bracket `(D/D0)^(2n)` is 1 for every order, so H = 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5. 0.61 is the Gaussian value at D0, and 1/6 wrongly uses 1/(1 + n).

questions.text: The book's Figure 4.11 marks the height of the Gaussian low-pass curves at D = D0 as 0.667. What does the formula `e^(-D²/2D0²)` really give there?
options: 0.667, as printed
About 0.607
questions.why: At D = D0 the exponent is -1/2, so H = e^(-0.5) ≈ 0.607 (the lecture rounds it to 0.61); the figure's 0.667 is a book error, flagged in the lecture's Check the source note. 0.5 is the Butterworth value and 0.368 = e^(-1).

questions.text: What happens to a Butterworth low-pass filter as its order n is increased?
options: It turns into a Gaussian filter and stops ringing entirely
It falls more steeply and rings more, like the ideal
It passes more than 0.5 at the cutoff D0
Its cutoff D0 moves outward in proportion to n
questions.why: The order sets how steeply H falls around D0, where it always passes 0.5. As n grows the filter approaches the ideal one, ringing included; n = 1 is gentle with no visible ringing.

questions.text: The book stresses one property of the Gaussian filter: the inverse Fourier transform of a Gaussian is ......
options: a ring-shaped lobe of alternating sign
a cylinder whose radius is D0
also a Gaussian, a single bump
a constant equal to the DC term
questions.why: The inverse of a Gaussian is also a Gaussian, one positive bump. By the convolution theorem, multiplying by H means convolving with that bump, so the Gaussian low-pass filter causes no ringing; rings belong to the ideal filter.

questions.text: Which formula is the Butterworth high-pass filter of order n?
questions.why: The BHPF puts D0/D in the bracket, and it equals 1 minus the BLPF: with r = D/D0, `1 - 1/(1 + r^(2n)) = 1/(1 + r^(-2n))`. D/D0 in the bracket is the low-pass filter, and so is 1 minus the high-pass.

questions.text: According to the book's comparison table of the three filter families, which pairing is correct?
options: Gaussian: has an order parameter n
Ideal: sharp cutoff and high ringing
Butterworth: no ringing at any order
Ideal: very smooth transition
questions.why: The table gives the ideal filter a sharp cutoff and high ringing, Butterworth a smooth adjustable transition, low ringing and the only order parameter n, and the Gaussian a very smooth transition with very low ringing.

questions.text: Why does the output of an ideal high-pass filter look dark everywhere except at the edges?
options: Its H = 0 at the centre removes the DC term, the mean level
H = 1 at the centre doubles the contrast of the flat areas
The inverse transform always returns negative pixel values
The cutoff D0 removes the highest frequencies, not the lowest
questions.why: The IHPF sets H = 0 for D ≤ D0, and that disc includes the DC term, the average brightness. Only edges and fine detail survive, on a dark background.

questions.text: In the frequency domain Gaussian low-pass `H = e^(-D²/2D0²)`, what happens to the blur when D0 is made larger?
options: More blur, as the book's σ = 0.5, 1, 2 figure shows
No change, since the Gaussian has no cutoff at all
More ringing appears, as with the ideal filter
Less blur, because more frequencies are kept
questions.why: A larger D0 widens H, so more frequencies pass and the image is blurred less. The book's second Figure 4.12 blurs more as σ grows only because there σ is the width of the spatial mask; the lecture's Check the source note explains this.

questions.text: Why is a spectrum usually displayed as `log(1 + abs(F))` instead of `abs(F)`?
options: The DC value dwarfs the rest, which would look black
`abs(F)` is still complex, so `imshow` cannot display it
The log moves the DC term into the centre of the display
The log removes the phase so that only the magnitude is left
questions.why: As the lecture's definition of the spectrum notes, the DC term is by far the largest value, so on a linear scale everything else would look black; the log compresses the range, and the 1 keeps zeros at 0. `abs` already returns a real array, and centring is `fftshift`'s job.

questions.text: Which MATLAB line computes the centred spectrum F of a grayscale image f, as steps 2 and 3 of the book's general steps require?
options: `F = ifft2(fftshift(f))`
`F = fftshift(ifft2(f))`
`F = fftshift(fft2(f))`
`F = fft2(ifftshift(f))`
questions.why: `fft2` computes F(u,v), then `fftshift` swaps its quadrants diagonally so the DC term moves to the centre. `ifft2` is the inverse transform, and shifting the image itself does not centre its spectrum.

questions.text: The spectrum was centred with `fftshift` and filtered with `G = H .* F`. Which MATLAB line gives the correct filtered image g?
options: `g = real(ifft2(G))`
`g = real(fft2(ifftshift(G)))`
`g = real(ifft2(ifftshift(G)))`
`g = real(ifft2(ifftshift(F)))`
questions.why: The shift must be undone with `ifftshift` before `ifft2`, and `real` drops the round-off imaginary part. Skipping `ifftshift` returns g·(-1)^(x+y) for even M and N, a checkerboard of signs; the book's step lists leave this out, so this follows the lecture's Check the source note.

questions.text: In the lecture's Python version, with D the distance array and D0 the cutoff, which line builds the Gaussian low-pass filter?
questions.why: `H = e^(-D²/2D0²)` is `np.exp(-D**2 / (2 * D0**2))`. Without the minus sign H grows with D, without the 2 the filter no longer passes 0.61 at D0, and 1 minus it is the Gaussian high-pass.
